title: Scientific Wiki Template
text:
This guide outlines the basic steps to set up, configure, and publish your own version of this Scientific Wiki.


First, fork this repository to your own GitHub account.



Forking the template


Once this is done, you will have the base template files in your new repository:



Initial repository files


To enable website hosting, you need to create an empty branch called gh-pages. Then, navigate to your repository settings, go to the GitHub Pages section, and select the gh-pages branch as your build and deployment source:



GitHub Pages setup





The main configuration for the website is handled inside the _quarto.yml file. You can customize this file to change the site’s title, logo, navigation sidebar, and bibliography settings:
website:
  title: "Scientific Wiki Template"
  search: true
  sidebar:
    style: "docked"
    logo: "img/logo/logo.png"
    contents:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: "Home"
      - section: "Topics"
        contents:
        - section: "Examples"
          contents:
          - auto: "doc/Examples/*.qmd"
        - section: "Physics"
          contents:
          - auto: "doc/Physics/*.qmd"
      - href: https://github.com/MKReyesH/ScientificWiki
        text: "GitHub Project"
      - href: about.qmd

bibliography: bib/references.bib
csl: bib/journal-of-cosmology-and-astroparticle-physics.csl
You can manage references by adding .bib files to the bib/ folder. You can also change the citation style by updating the csl file path. Quarto supports many Zotero styles, which can be found at the Zotero Style Repository.



Bibliography files





To add new pages to the wiki, simply create new plain text files (with .qmd extension) inside the doc/ folder. The system will automatically recognize the files and add them to the sidebar. The sidebar reproduces the exact folder structure inside the doc/ folder, so you can create drop-down menus simply by placing files inside sub-folders:



Documentation folder structure


All content files must be plain text file using the .qmd extension and must be written using Quarto Markdown syntax. For a detailed guide on native formatting, please see the Quarto Markdown Guide.
Moreover, anticipating that a lot of scientific content is already written in LaTeX, this template also includes (limited) compatibility for simple LaTeX structures. The commands that are safe to use in the .qmd files are explained in the Allowed LaTeX Syntax Guide. For more complex structures like figures or tables, native Markdown syntax must be used.



Every time you commit changes to your repository, GitHub Actions will automatically take care of the deployment phase. The updated webpage will be built and pushed to the gh-pages branch, going live online in just a few minutes.

title: How to create dynamic tables
text: Standard Markdown tables, as shown in the Quarto Markdown Guide, work well for small static datasets. For larger scientific tables requiring live search, sorting, unit conversions, LaTeX math, or literature references, this template provides a custom dynamic-tables filter that renders interactive Tabulator tables directly from .csv files.

title: How to create dynamic tables
text:
Global Options
Global options are specified as key: value pairs at the top of the block:

src: Path to the input .csv file (required).
searchable: Shows or hides the full-row search bar above the table (true or false, default false).
sortable: Enables or disables sorting across all columns (true or false, default true).
per-page: Sets the initial number of rows per page (default 15, with a selector for 10, 15, 25, and 50 rows). The pagination footer hides automatically whenever the active row count fits within one page.

title: How to create dynamic tables
text:
Column Options
Individual columns are configured with col N:, using a 0-based index (col 0: is the first column, col 1: is the second, and so on). Multiple properties for the same column are separated by commas:

header=...: Replaces the CSV header title. Enclose the title in quotes ("..." or '...') if it contains commas; inline math expressions (such as header=$m$) are also supported when latex or latexnum is active (see below).
number / string: Enforces numeric or alphabetical sorting instead of auto-detection (empty cells always sort to the bottom). Numeric columns automatically format extreme magnitudes (\(\vert{}x\vert{} < 10^{-3}\) or \(\vert{}x\vert{} \ge 10^4\)) in exponential notation.
sortable / unsortable: Overrides the global sortable setting for that column.
latex: Renders any LaTeX math syntax ($ ... $, $$ ... $$, \( ... \), or \[ ... \]) in both the column header and cell text via MathJax or KaTeX.
dropdown: Adds a filter menu in the column header populated with all unique values in that column.

::: {.dynamic-table}
src: data/example-table.csv
searchable: true
per-page: 4
col 0: header="Sector", dropdown
col 1: header="Particle", latex
col 2: header="Mass [GeV]", number
col 3: header="Discovery", unsortable
:::

title: How to create dynamic tables
section: Scientific Units, LaTeX Math Numbers, and INSPIRE-HEP Citations
text:
Scientific Units, LaTeX Math Numbers, and INSPIRE-HEP Citations
Three specialized column tags support physical unit scaling, LaTeX scientific notation, and automated bibliography management:

units(Unit1: factor1, Unit2: factor2, ...): Implies number and adds a unit selector to the column header. The first unit listed is active by default; selecting another unit multiplies every numeric cell in the column by its conversion factor.
latexnum: Implies both number and latex, and transforms numeric cells into inline math expressions (1.057e-1 displayed as \(1.06 \times 10^{-1}\)) that update automatically whenever the user switches units.
inspire: Implies string and treats cell values as INSPIRE-HEP TeX citation keys (multiple keys in one cell can be separated by commas or semicolons, with or without a leading @). During compilation, the filter fetches the corresponding BibTeX records from INSPIRE-HEP in batches, turns each valid key into a clickable [N] CitationKey link that highlights the target entry on click, and renders a live reference list directly below the table that updates as rows are searched, filtered, or paginated.

::: {.dynamic-table}
src: data/example-table.csv
searchable: true
per-page: 4
col 0: header="Sector", dropdown
col 1: header="Particle", latex
col 2: header=$m$, latexnum, units(GeV: 1, MeV: 1e3, TeV: 1e-3)
col 3: header="Discovery", inspire, unsortable
:::





\(\)

text:
About us

Powered By

GitHub Pages: Hosting and deployment infrastructure.
Quarto: Markdown rendering, cross-referencing, and website generation.
Pandoc: Document format translation.
Bootstrap and Bootswatch: CSS support and user interface.
MathJax: Mathematical notation rendering.
Gemini: Help writing the Lua filters.



Contributing
If you would like to contribute to the core template, add new LaTeX translation rules, or fix a bug, do not hesitate to open a Pull Request at the GitHub Repository.

title: How to write a page
text: GitHub Pages transforms plain text files into HTML webpages. In this template, files use the .qmd extension and follow Quarto Markdown syntax. Below are examples of the most commonly used formatting structures.

title: How to write a page
text:
This is a subsection

This is a sub-subsection
To make a section cross-referenceable, append an identifier starting with #sec- to the header. For example, typing ## Mathematical Equations {#sec-maths} allows the section to be referenced anywhere in the document using @sec-maths.

title: How to create dynamic plots
text: Static figures, as shown in the Quarto Markdown Guide, work well for fixed illustrations. For interactive scientific plots requiring zoomable 2D/3D canvases, analytical curve evaluation, tabular data overlays, LaTeX math labels, or animated parameter sweeps, this template provides a custom dynamic-plots filter powered by Plotly.

title: How to create dynamic plots
text:
Analytical Functions
Use ::: {.plot-function id="..."} to evaluate analytical expressions. Expressions support +, -, *, /, ^, implicit multiplication (2x, x sin(x)), constants (pi, e), and standard functions (sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, log, ln, log10, log2, sqrt, abs, sign, floor, ceil, min, max):

expr: Mathematical expression (required). Whether = is present determines how the expression is evaluated:

Explicit (no =): Defines \(y = f(x)\) in 2D (using x) or \(z = f(x, y)\) in 3D (using x and y). Explicit expressions cannot contain z. 2D explicit curves sample along xrange only and automatically resample when zooming or panning.
Implicit (contains one =): Defines a 2D contour \(f(x, y) = g(x, y)\) (using x and y) or a 3D isosurface \(f(x, y, z) = g(x, y, z)\) (using x, y, and z). Because implicit equations are solved on a grid, they use sampling bounds along every active variable (xrange and yrange in 2D; xrange, yrange, and zrange in 3D), and mode and smooth are ignored.

xrange, yrange, zrange: Sampling domain [min, max] (min < max) along each axis (default: the canvas range if set, otherwise the co-plotted file extent, or [-10, 10]).
points: Sample resolution per axis, integer \(\ge 2\) (defaults: 100 for 2D explicit, 60 per axis for 2D implicit and 3D explicit, 25 per axis for 3D implicit).
label: Legend title, supporting inline LaTeX math (default: the block’s id).
color: Trace or surface color, passed directly as any valid CSS/Plotly color string (default: automatic colorway).
mode: Drawing style for explicit 2D curves (lines, markers, or lines+markers, default lines).
smooth: Enables spline interpolation between sample points on explicit 2D curves (true or false, default true).

title: How to create dynamic plots
text:
Data Files
Use ::: {.plot-file id="..."} to plot numeric columns from .csv (comma-separated) or whitespace/tab-delimited text files (blank lines and comment lines starting with #, %, or // are ignored automatically):

src: Path to the input data file (required).
skip: Number of leading non-comment header rows to ignore, integer \(\ge 0\) (default 0).
x: Column expression for the horizontal axis using 0-based column tokens (c0, c1, c2, …) and any supported math operators, constants, or functions (required).
y: Vertical-axis column expression in standard mode (e.g., c1 or sqrt(c1^2 + c2^2)), or the sweep column selection when param is set (required).
z: Column expression for the third axis in 3D scatter/line traces (e.g., c2). Cannot be combined with param.
label: Legend title, supporting inline LaTeX math (default: the block’s id).
color: Trace color, passed directly as any valid CSS/Plotly color string (default: automatic colorway).
mode: Drawing style (lines, markers, or lines+markers, default lines+markers).
smooth: Enables spline interpolation between points on 2D line traces (true or false, default false).
Parameter sweep keys (enabled when param is provided; param-label and transform require param):

param: Numeric parameter values mapped one-to-one onto the columns selected by y. Set y to an ascending column range (c1..c7) or an explicit comma-separated list (c1, c3, c5, c7), and specify param either as a uniform range start..end (0..3, which interpolates linearly across at least 2 columns) or as a matching comma-separated list (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0).
param-label: Label displayed next to the active parameter value above the slider, supporting inline LaTeX math (default Parameter).
transform: Optional mathematical expression applied to every sweep column value before plotting. Inside transform, y refers to the active sweep column’s value in that row, and any column token (c0, c1, …) from the same row may also be referenced (for example, transform: y^2 to plot squared amplitude, or transform: y / c1 to normalize against c1).


::: {.plot-file id="damped-data"}
src: data/example-plot-damped.csv
skip: 1
x: c0
y: c1
label: Measured amplitude
mode: markers
color: #ff7f0e
:::

::: {.plot-function id="damped-model"}
expr: exp(-0.35 * x) * cos(2 * x)
label: $e^{-0.35t}\cos(2t)$
color: #1f77b4
:::

::: {.dynamic-plot}
curves: damped-data, damped-model
xlabel: Time $t$ [s]
ylabel: Amplitude $A(t)$ [m]
:::

title: How to create dynamic plots
text:
Plot Canvas
The ::: {.dynamic-plot} block mounts the responsive Plotly canvas and configures axes and interactive controls:

curves: Comma-separated list of .plot-function and/or .plot-file IDs to display together (required). All curves in a plot must share the same dimensionality (all 2D or all 3D), with at most one parameter-sweep curve per canvas.
xlabel, ylabel, zlabel: Axis titles, supporting inline LaTeX math ($ ... $, \( ... \)). In 3D scenes, axes default to x, y, and z.
xscale, yscale, zscale: Axis scaling (linear or log, default linear).
xrange, yrange, zrange: Initial visible axis bounds formatted as [min, max] (min < max; bounds must be strictly positive when the corresponding axis uses log scale).
width, height: Canvas dimensions in pixels, integer \(\ge 200\). height defaults to 400; when width is omitted, the canvas automatically adapts to the available container width.
legend: Shows or hides the collapsible right-hand legend sidebar with per-curve visibility checkboxes (true or false, default true; when false, no legend is shown).
play: Adds a Play/Pause animation toggle button next to the parameter slider (true or false, default false). Valid only when curves includes a parameter-sweep curve.

title: How to create dynamic plots
text:
Animated Parameter Sweeps
Combining sweep options in .plot-file with play: true in .dynamic-plot creates an interactive slider plot:
::: {.plot-file id="wave-sweep"}
src: data/example-plot-sweep.csv
x: c0
y: c1..c7
param: 0..3
param-label: $t$ [s]
label: Wave amplitude
smooth: true
:::

::: {.dynamic-plot}
curves: wave-sweep
xlabel: $x$ [m]
ylabel: $\psi(x, t)$
play: true
:::




\(\)

title: How to use LaTeX syntax
text: In the scientific community, it is very common to have texts, equations, and full documents already written in LaTeX. This implies that one needs to translate such content to the Quarto Markdown syntax explained in the previous guide. However, this template allows for the use of some simple LaTeX syntax (in combination with native syntax), which is converted on the fly to the correct Quarto Markdown format. This document serves as both a guide and a test file for the translation rules. It is written using the supported LaTeX commands to explain exactly how the transformation works.

title: How to use LaTeX syntax
text:
This is a subsection

This is a sub-subsection
Because the script converts this directly into native Markdown, the system automatically generates a reference identifier for it based on the heading’s name (lowercase, using hyphens instead of spaces). This allows you to easily link back to the translated section using standard Markdown linking, such as typing [this section](#sections-and-subsections) to navigate back to this section.
